summary: Formal language describing text patterns: character classes, greedy and lazy quantifiers, lookarounds, and capture groups.

rows.means: matches any single character except newline
rows.consequence: To match a literal dot (like in a domain name or file extension), you must escape it with a backslash: \..

rows.means: zero or more occurrences / one or more occurrences
rows.consequence: Quantifiers are greedy by default: a.*b will match from the very first 'a' to the very last 'b' in the entire document.

rows.means: matches zero or one occurrence of the preceding element
rows.consequence: https? matches both 'http' and 'https'. Also used after * or + to make them lazy (non-greedy).

rows.means: anchors matching the start of string / end of string
rows.consequence: ^\d+$ matches an entire string of digits from start to finish, preventing matching digits buried inside text.

rows.means: matches any one character inside the set / negated set
rows.consequence: [^0-9] matches any single character that is not a digit.

rows.means: character range matching lowercase letters or digits
rows.consequence: Hyphens represent ranges inside brackets unless placed at the start or end of the bracket expression.

rows.means: shorthand character classes (digit, word, whitespace) and their inverses
rows.consequence: \d matches a digit, \w a word character, \s whitespace; the capitalised forms match everything the lower-case one does not.

rows.means: zero-width assertion between a word character (\w) and non-word
rows.consequence: \bcat\b matches the standalone word 'cat', but will not match 'catalog' or 'scatter'.

rows.means: groups sub-patterns together and captures matched text
rows.consequence: Parentheses both group a sub-pattern and capture what it matched, which is why adding brackets for precedence quietly renumbers everything after them.

rows.means: groups sub-patterns without allocating capture memory
rows.consequence: Optimizes regex execution performance when you need grouping for quantifiers (e.g. (?:abc)+) but don't need the matched text.

rows.means: captures matched text into a named group
rows.consequence: Reading a group by name rather than by position, which survives someone adding a bracket earlier in the pattern — the failure that numeric groups invite.

rows.means: asserts that what follows matches pattern without consuming characters
rows.consequence: \d+(?=px) matches digits only if they are immediately followed by 'px', but does not include 'px' in the match.

rows.means: asserts that what follows does not match the pattern
rows.consequence: foo(?!bar) matches foo only where bar does not follow. The assertion consumes nothing, so the position after the match is unchanged.
(?<=\$)\d+ matches numbers immediately preceded by a dollar sign without including the dollar sign.

rows.means: matches either pattern a or pattern b
rows.consequence: Evaluated from left to right: (cat|dog) matches either animal.

rows.means: exact repetition count / bounded repetition range
rows.consequence: \d{4} matches exactly 4 digits; \d{2,4} matches between 2 and 4 digits.

rows.code:
<.*?>   lazy      -- one tag
<.*>    greedy    -- first < to last >
rows.means: matches as few characters as possible to satisfy the pattern
rows.consequence: The lazy form stops at the first thing that satisfies the pattern; the greedy form takes as much as it can and gives back only when forced. Most surprising matches are this distinction.
g finds all matches; i ignores case; m makes ^ and $ match line starts/ends; s allows . to match newline characters.
